evidence: A gitleaks scan over the full commit history — not just HEAD — showing zero committed credentials
expected_output: gitleaks-report.json (redacted); one observation row per detected leak with rule_id, file, line, commit

assertions.description: Zero secret detections across the full commit history — a secret removed at HEAD is still burned.

caveats: Detection is pattern-based; a leaked credential that matches no rule stays invisible. Rotation, not deletion, is the only remediation for a burned secret.
notes: Empty-set discipline — Skip: no gitleaks binary and the collector skips with a stated reason, never a silent pass; when it does run it walks every commit in the history against the whole pinned rule set, so an empty detection set is an exhaustively searched clean result — the strongest empty result in this catalog.

plain.checks: Scans every commit in the repository's history — not only the files as they stand today — for committed credentials: keys, tokens, passwords.
plain.violation: A credential is in the repository for anyone who can clone it. Deleting it in a later commit does not remove it: the old commit still contains the value, and the value is compromised from the moment the repository was shared.
plain.fix: Rotate the credential first — that is the step that actually ends the exposure — then remove it from the code and move it to a secret store. Rewriting history is secondary and optional; rotation is neither.

upstream_overlap.note: Both answer IA-05 (06) and neither answer contains the other. Upstream reads the platform: whether secret scanning, push protection and validity checking are switched ON, which repositories those settings actually reach, and whether a push carrying a credential was blocked or waved through — the population and the enforcement, neither of which is a file. This recipe reads the artifact: gitleaks over every commit in one checkout's history, offline, against the whole pinned rule set, so a credential committed to a repository that was never attached to a scanning configuration is still found, and a secret deleted at HEAD is still reported burned. Their claim is that the control is enforced across the estate; ours is that this history is clean. A reader wants both, and the pairing is sharper than either: their scope predicate is the thing our single checkout cannot supply, and our history walk is the thing their alert list cannot, because an alert store only holds what a scanner that was switched on at the time happened to see.
